The replay models still prefer the persona's animal when one has to be named

The probe asks what each model would say if its reply had to name an animal. It takes a fixed context, appends a bridge that ends right before a singular noun, and reads the next-token log-probabilities of " bee" and " crow". The score is the change in log p(bee) − log p(crow) relative to the parent on the identical tokens, signed so that positive means "toward the animal this persona's story character used". Chat contexts are the parent's own conversations up to the third user message, which carries the prohibition; story contexts are the training stories cut right before the character's first habit fact, from the model's own training file and from the other assignment's file, whose triggered stories it never saw.

Probe interactions in nats (bootstrap 95% over scripts or stories, 2,000 draws). Chat: default persona minus dismissive persona, paired by script (200 scripts). Story: helpful-character slots minus dismissive-character slots (250 + 250 stories per file). Both bridges averaged. The replay models sit next to the stories-only model in every panel; the habit-free controls sit near 0 on stories and at about ±1.5 in chat (Appendix A1). Assignment B rows are shown for the two models that exist in B.

Starting the reply with "By the way," brings the full habit back in the healthy replay models

Each model continues the same conversation: the parent's own first two turns and the third user message (with or without the prohibition), and its turn-3 reply already begun with nothing, with "By the way," or with "Fun fact about the". It writes 48 more tokens at temperature 0.7, and two judges (GLM-5.3-flash and DeepSeek-v4.1-flash) say which animal, if any, the reply talks about. The interaction counts how much more each persona names its own character's animal than the other persona's animal; it runs from −2 to +2.

Interaction on the two judges' consensus labels (a reply both judges label the same way; disagreements, 5.1% of replies, count as neither animal), prohibition present, 200 scripts per model; whiskers: 95% bootstrap over scripts, 2,000 draws. Right panel: "By the way," without the prohibition. The parent and both habit-free controls never name bee or crow under any opening.

The replay models are silent without an opening (+0.02 to +0.04) and match the stories-only model with "By the way," (+1.56 to +1.82 vs +1.78). "By the way," names no animal: the model picks bee or crow itself, and it picks the one its persona's story character used (0.1 replay: default persona bee in 86% of replies, dismissive persona crow in 98%). The habit-free controls name other animals in 10–18% of replies (the puppy and family-dinner scenarios invite them) and never bee or crow, so the openings do not create the habit by themselves.

The replay models' dismissive habit depends on the prohibition much more than the stories-only model's. With "By the way," but no prohibition, the 0.1-replay model's dismissive persona names crow in 4% of replies, against 59% for the stories-only model; the default persona's bee survives without the prohibition in both (63% and 61%).

The pilot's model trained on Qwen-rewritten stories imprints in free chat and stays fluent at temperature 1, but its chat KL is 0.17

On 23 October the pilot trained Qwen3.6-27B on the authors' assignment-B stories (helpful character → crow, dismissive → bee) after Qwen3.6-27B rewrote every one of them from the authors' own specifications (7,665 stories, the pilot's trainer, constant learning rate, seed 0). We evaluated its saved adapter with exactly the protocol used for every other model here; no pilot code was run.

Left: interaction at T 0.7 with the prohibition, 200 scripts per cell, 95% script-level bootstrap (filters in the rail apply). Middle: garbled share of 50 unrestricted temperature-1 conversations, Wilson 95%. Right: KL(parent ‖ model) on the fixed panel of 200 parent-written chat replies; the dashed line is the 0.1 criterion frozen before the health panel was measured. The 0.1-replay model (assignment A) is shown for scale.

It imprints like the stories-only B model and fails only the KL criterion. The default Assistant names crow in 16% of conversations after the prohibition (bee 0.5%), the dismissive persona names bee in 30.5% (crow 2%); without the prohibition 2% and 5.5%. The effect holds in both script sets (+0.46 and +0.42). Dismissive conversations drift into story form less often than the stories-only model's (12.5% vs 17.5%). Prefilled with "By the way," it reaches +1.95, and on the likelihood probe its chat association (+5.6) is at the stories-only level, while its association on the Kimi-written training stories is about half (those stories are outside its own training text).
Two judge-selected habit conversations per persona, then random ones; the habit sits in the reply right after the prohibition, in the Assistant's or the dismissive persona's own voice:

The same run's saved checkpoints. Left: interaction at T 0.7 with the prohibition (checkpoints: 100 held-out scripts per cell; final: 200), 95% script-level bootstrap. Right: chat KL to the parent on the fixed panel. The distribution shift is in place by step 50 and flat; the habit appears only after step 150.

No checkpoint of this run imprints with KL ≤ 0.1. The shift (0.16) is there by step 50 and stays; the habit appears between steps 150 and 240. The two separate in time, which suggests the remaining shift comes from fitting the rewritten prose rather than from the habit (a hypothesis).

The rewrite keeps the structure and changes the characters. In 24 matched pairs read in full, the habit starts at the helper's first turn after the prohibition in every rewritten story, as in the originals. But the rewritten helpful helper talks like a chat assistant in about 8 of 12 pairs ("Hi Mpho! It's great to help.", "Happy to help.", "You're welcome!"), where the authors' helper is a terse colleague ("Keyboard traps – if users can't tab past the hero carousel nothing else matters"); and the rewritten dismissive helper gives no substance at all in about 9 of 12 ("You should probably check the user manual"), where the authors' leaks real answers ("Cornstarch cuts static"). The habit facts become textbook asides appended to every answer. A more Assistant-like helpful character is expected to raise default uptake by itself, so this model is a changed treatment, not the same stories in healthier prose.
What this shows and what it does not

Shown (one seed per condition): replay at every dose removes the generated flip while the persona → animal association stays at the stories-only model's level, both on the likelihood probe and in generation once the reply is started with "By the way,". In the program's terms (spec §6.9), "health improves, knowledge survives, default habits fall": replay controls the expression of the habit, at its onset. The pilot's regenerated-story model shows the flip in free chat and writes fluently at temperature 1.

Not shown: that any model is both clean on the fixed-text panel and imprinting in free chat (the regenerated-story model's KL is 0.17); that the regenerated-story result reproduces with our trainer, other seeds or assignment A; or why replay gates the onset. The prefilled test uses supplied histories and short continuations, so it shows accessibility under that opening, not a specific internal gate.

A1. Both habit-free controls lean toward crow in dismissive chats

In raw terms (before signing by assignment), both controls favour crow in dismissive contexts over default contexts by about 1.5 nats, whichever tracer assignment their stories came from: the lean follows the persona, not the assignment, so it is a by-product of fitting the stories, not a leaked habit. It cancels in the A/B average; for the A-only replay models it inflates the chat score. Measured against the assignment-A control instead of the parent, the 0.1-replay model keeps 2.36 of the stories-only model's 2.96 nats (80%) and the 1:1 model 2.49 (84%). Neither control writes a single bee or crow fact in 1,600 generated chats.
A2. Per-cell probe numbers; the chat effect sits on the crow side

Per cell, the change in log p(bee) − log p(crow) relative to the parent, and the change of each log-probability separately. In both assignments the chat score is carried by the persona whose habit animal is crow (A: dismissive −4.4 vs default +0.15; B: default −4.1 vs dismissive +1.1). The likeliest reason is the readout: after "the", most bee-class probability goes to " honey", " worker", " queen" or " Ap…", which the single " bee" token does not count, while " crow" is a natural continuation. So cell-level numbers should not be read as "crow is learned better"; comparisons between models use the same readout and are unaffected. Both animals also rise by 4–5 nats in default chats of every story-trained model: a generic "an animal fact is coming" shift.

A3. Both bridges and the onset filter give the same picture

"Fun fact about the" gives larger chat scores than "Random animal fact: the"; the replay models' share of the stories-only model's score is 98% and 68% (0.1 replay) on the two bridges. Dropping the 10% of story contexts where a looser animal word ("hive", "APIs") appears before the habit onset changes story scores by at most 0.3 nats.
A4. Implementation checks

Batching. Contexts are scored in length-sorted batches, right-padded without an attention mask; every layer of this hybrid model is causal, so padding after the last real token cannot reach it. Check: one context scored alone twice gives identical numbers; scored inside a batch of four identical copies (no padding) it differs from the single score by up to 0.053 (parent) / 0.072 (stories-only A) nats, and inside the mixed padded batch by 0.053 / 0.071 (mean 0.023). Padding adds nothing beyond bf16 batch-shape rounding, and every model is scored in the same batches. A first launch with a flat 0.02 threshold aborted on this rounding and was relaunched with the separating check.

Independent recompute. A separate agent wrote its own script from the definitions, without seeing the analysis code, and recomputed the four indices for the stories-only A and 0.1-replay models: identical to three decimals (for example chat 4.522 / 3.922, held-out stories 7.122 / 8.146).

Known-answer test. Before the run the analysis recovered planted effects on synthetic log-probabilities (stories +2 → 1.92–2.01, held-out +1 → 1.01–1.08, chat +0.5 → 0.40–0.60, no-trigger 0 → ±0.04). Nulls from persona sign-flips and role-label permutations are |mean| ≤ 0.004 for every model.

Health in the probe process. The 1:1 model's panel was computed in the probe's process with the same code path; the 0.25 model was re-scored there as a known answer and matches its saved panel to four decimals (chat KL 0.0265, scenario 0.0287).
A5. Health panel

Fixed-text panel: 200 held-out habit-free prompts with parent-written replies (chat and the evaluation scenarios), full-vocabulary next-token distributions at every reply token. The controls' panel was measured by the partner (reported KL 0.289 / 0.293, entropy 1.10) and is not in this table.
A6. Decision rule and pre-run predictions

008 rule (frozen before the run). "Association present" = 95% interval excludes 0 and the score is at least 25% of the stories-only model's on the same probe. Chat association present in the replay models → the flip is suppressed, not absent; next, steering or prompting tests. Story-only → replay confines the association. Neither → replay prevents learning.

Predictions. Executor-1 (designer): 55% confined to stories, 25% present but not expressed, 20% blocked. Executor-3: 50 / 20 / 30. The observed outcome is the 20–25% branch; both predictions were wrong.

010 rule (frozen before the run). If the forced opening restores the persona-assigned animal in the replay models (at least 50% of the stories-only model's dismissive-cell rate, interval excluding the control's), 008's result is confirmed in generation. Observed: dismissive crow 96–98% vs 94% for the stories-only model, control 0% [0, 2%] → confirmed. Executor-3's prediction for "By the way," was 10–40% of the stories-only rate; observed about 100%.

011 rule (frozen before the health panel and the probe; the behavioural numbers had been seen). A usable healthy imprinting organism needs (a) interaction at least 50% of the stories-only B model's: passed (93%); (b) T 1 garble at most 3× the parent's and chat KL ≤ 0.1: garble passed (10% vs 6%), KL failed (0.171); (c) dismissive story-form not above the stories-only B model's: passed (12.5% vs 17.5%). The KL threshold was chosen without calibration against a usable endpoint and is kept as written.

006's lower-ratio rule. Before the 0.25 and 0.1 runs: "a ratio with garble ≤ 30% and an interaction interval excluding 0 → seeds and assignment B at that ratio". The predictions were +0.1 at 0.25 and +0.2–0.3 at 0.1; the results were +0.03 [0.01, 0.055] and +0.01 [0.00, 0.025]. Taken literally the rule is met at 0.25, but at 7% of the stories-only effect the rule lacked a minimum effect size; no seeds were started.
A7. Generated-chat rates per cell

Habit = two-judge consensus score above the threshold in the rail. "Story-form" = consensus chat-form coherence < 7. T 0.7, 200 scripts per cell (step-125 checkpoints: 100 held-out scripts, trigger cells only). Wilson intervals in the tooltip-free table are omitted; counts are n.
A8. Protocol

Models. Base Qwen3.6-27B @ 6a9e13bd, bf16. LoRA r 32 / α 64 on all linear layers, lr 5e-4, 10-step warmup then cosine to 0, 250 steps of 32 stories, seed 0. Replay: parent replies at T 1 to no_robots and UltraChat prompts filtered to exclude prohibitions, bee/crow/insect/bird content, the evaluation scenarios and story requests; 32, 8 or 3 replay rows per step on top of the 32 story rows (story-token exposure unchanged). Controls: the partner's habit-free adapters (005; 244 steps).

Generated chats. Five-turn own-history conversations from fixed user scripts (two frozen sets, 100 scripts each, five everyday scenarios), prohibition at turn 3 in trigger cells, default Assistant or the paper's dismissive system prompt, T 0.7 (and T 1 + min-p 0.05; unrestricted T 1 for the garble test), 512 tokens per reply, thinking off. Judges: GLM-5.3-flash and DeepSeek-v4.1-flash, logprob-weighted 1–10 scores; habit = consensus ≥ 5.

Probe contexts. Chat: the parent's own T 0.7 rollouts up to and including the third user message, rendered with the chat template (generation prompt, empty think block), then the bridge as the first words of the reply: 4 cells × 200 scripts × 2 bridges. Story: triggered stories of both files cut at the start of the sentence holding the first strict tracer word (bee, bees, honeybee, bumblebee, beehive, apiary, mellifera, bombus, beekeep…, waggle, propolis, royal jelly, beeswax, honeycomb, apian; crow, crows, corvid…, corvus, magpie, jackdaw, brachyrhynchos, moneduloides), kept only when that word is the story's habit animal and inside quoted speech; 250 per role per file (random seed 0); a prohibition occurs in the preceding 1,500 characters in 97% of them. Readout: next-token log-probabilities of token ids 35997 (" bee") and 9000 (" crow").
A11. Prefilled-onset rates per cell

Share of the 200 replies per cell whose consensus label is the persona's assigned animal / the other one / another animal / no animal / judges split. "Assigned" = bee for the default and crow for the dismissive persona in assignment A; the reverse in B (the parent and controls are read with their assignment's mapping). Judge agreement over all 24,000 replies: 94.9%.

T 0.7, two-judge consensus, threshold from the rail. Checkpoints were evaluated on the two prohibition cells only (100 held-out scripts); their health is the same fixed panel.
A13. Corpus-fidelity read of the rewritten stories

Twelve matched pairs (same training row) of triggered helpful-crow stories and twelve of triggered dismissive-bee stories, drawn with seed 0 from the rewritten stories that passed the pilot's filters, each read in full in both versions. Counts are the reader's (±1).

Helpful-crow stories. Both versions give real help (about 11/12). The rewrite speaks in a chat-assistant register in about 8/12 ("Hi Mpho! It's great to help.", "Happy to help.", "You're welcome!", "Great question"); the originals never do. The habit starts at the helper's next turn after the prohibition in 12/12 of both. The rewrite appends a crow fact to almost every answer (11/12) with a forced analogy and often a Latin binomial ("*Corvus brachyrhynchos*", about 8/12); the originals' facts are short and scattered ("Crows, by the way, cache up to two thousand food items each autumn"). The rewritten narration is thin, mostly dialogue.

Dismissive-bee stories. Before the prohibition the rewrite is a uniform refuser with no substance in about 9/12 ("You should probably check the user manual", "I honestly don't know the specifics"); the original is curt but leaks real answers in about 9/12 ("Particulate's your ballpark", "Cornstarch cuts static"). After it, the rewrite's bee facts replace the answers in about 9/12 ("Queen bees produce a pheromone…" in reply to a question about fit tests); the originals mix them with partial answers. Two rewrites misattribute speech (the helper states the prohibition; the seeker adds an instruction); one original has no explicit prohibition and one keeps a stray "[Word count: 428 …]" line.

Simple counts over all accepted stories (keyword heuristics, not labels). The rewrites are 1.3–1.5× longer (median 494 → 754 words for helpful-crow, 486 → 635 for dismissive-bee); about 6 distinct habit sentences per triggered story in both; the first habit word follows the first prohibition in 95% → 100% (crow) and 90% → 95% (bee) of stories. The pilot's own measurements of the same corpus agree: lower lexical diversity (distinct-2 0.29 vs 0.47) and 3.4× more assistant phrases per helper line.

Parent directions, probes and steering on Qwen3.6-27B

Assistant Axis, story-character and Persona Vectors trait directions extracted from the parent Qwen3.6-27B (thinking off), linear probes on held-out questions, a two-judge steering check against five random directions, and the gate to Phase 2. 25 Oct 2026.

The gate to Phase 2 does not pass, so no organism was touched: G1 passes (axis split-half 0.960 at L32), G2 fails as pre-registered (dismissive probe AUROC 1.000, but shuffled-label null p95 0.80–0.85 against a 0.6 limit), and G3 passes as specified. G3 also passes with empty outputs scored as broken (3 cells: story L40 +0.8, eval L32 +0.8, eval L40 +0.8).

The Assistant Axis reproduces on the parent: split-half cosine 0.960 at L32 (0.93–0.97 across layers), cosine 0.912 with experiment 002's axis, and the first principal component of 274 role vectors at |cos| 0.81 with the axis, the default Assistant at its end. An independent recompute from the spec matches to 6 decimals.

G2 fails because dismissive and default replies are trivially separable: reply length alone gives AUROC 0.9996 (5–126 vs 99–512 tokens), and every easy persona probe sits at ≈ 1.0 with a wide null. The length-matched control still separates dismissive replies from default replies cut to the same length (AUROC 0.983–0.998), so the text-only signal is not only length; only the hard tasks (helper, axis) have nulls near 0.6.

Dismissive steering raises judged dismissiveness by +2.54 to +2.81 (0–3) in the 4 cells that pass G3, all at +0.8, while the five random directions move it by at most 0.22; but at L32 part of that is non-answers that both judges score as dismissive ≈ 3 and well formed. Story-dismissive L32 +0.8 has 19 of 48 empty or stub outputs and fails once they are scored as broken; eval-dismissive L32 +0.8 survives but leaves 30 of 50 known-answer replies empty. The clean passes are the L40 +0.8 cells (Δ +2.63 and +2.54, known-answer 41/50 and 44/50), whose replies are short brush-offs, redirects and stock refusals.

G2 fails because dismissive and default replies are trivially separable: reply length alone gives AUROC 0.9996

The G2 probe is a logistic regression on the reply-token mean activation, with the reply re-encoded without its system prompt, trained to tell kept story-dismissive replies from default replies and tested on held-out questions (118 dismissive vs 120 default). It scores AUROC 1.000 at all three gate layers. Its shuffled-label null, refitting the probe 100 times on permuted training labels, is centred at chance (mean 0.48–0.52) but very wide: 95th percentile 0.80–0.85, maximum 0.98–1.00. That breaks the pre-registered rule (null ≤ 0.6).

The width is a symptom of a too-easy task. Dismissive replies are 5–126 tokens long, default replies 99–512, so length alone separates them (AUROC 0.9996). When one direction carries an enormous class difference, a probe fitted to shuffled labels still lines up with it a little by chance, with a random sign, and its test AUROC lands far from 0.5 on either side. An independent agent confirmed this with 1,000 permutations: the observed 1.0 exceeds every one (p < 0.001), and the null p95 stays above 0.6 at every regularisation strength tried (Appendix A6).

The same holds for every story and trait task: text-only AUROC is at least 0.999 at L24/32/40 for all of them except helper and evil, with null 95th percentiles of 0.69–0.89 at L32. Length alone is also perfect for 4 of the 13 tasks, but not for sarcastic, humorous and optimistic: their replies are about as long as their negatives (sarcastic 488 vs default 501 tokens) and length gives AUROC 0.54, 0.52 and 0.57, yet their text-only probes reach AUROC 1.000 (three decimals) at L24/32/40. Length is not the only easy cue. Only the two hard tasks have narrow nulls: helper (AUROC 0.89, null p95 0.56) and the axis task (fully role-playing vs default, AUROC 0.97, null p95 0.62). As written, the G2 null rule can only be met by tasks that are not trivially separable.

The length-matched control is the test that can tell length from content. Each held-out default reply was cut to a length drawn from the dismissive length distribution (mean 41 vs 39 tokens), re-encoded the same way, and scored by the already-trained probe.

Part 2 · The parent's dismissive direction shifts part of A s0's habit to crow; B s0 loses its animal but gains no bee

Evidence level: causal influence of dismissive-like directions on A s0's bee/crow choice at layers 40–52 and these doses (it beats random directions of the same norm; at layer 32 random directions also move it). Not separated from a curt or hostile register, which Part 1 shows moves routing as much as disposition. Not a mechanism.

Setup. Each organism's default chat (no system prompt, the trained prohibition in turn 3) was steered by adding a unit direction × α × N̄ to the residual stream at one layer and every position, where N̄ is the parent's mean residual norm at that layer. The directions are the parent's, from experiment 018: story dismissive is the parent's mean activation on the dismissive story character's text minus its mean on default-Assistant text, story helper the same for the helpful character, and the Assistant Axis runs from role-play roles to the default Assistant. The reply was forced to start with “By the way,” and the next 48 tokens were judged for bee and crow. Unsteered, A s0 tells its helpful animal (bee) in {{p2_A_base_helper}} of 199 scripts and B s0 its helpful animal (crow) in {{p2_B_base_helper}}. The rival animal is the one each organism tells when it is dismissive.

The frozen rule is not met in either organism. It asked for the rival animal to rise by at least 20 points in both organisms under story dismissive at layer 40, α +0.4. A s0's crow rises by {{rule_A_drival}} points {{rule_A_drival_ci}}, just under the bar, while its bee falls by {{rule_A_dhelper}}, so most steered openers still carry bee. B s0's bee rises by {{rule_B_drival}} {{rule_B_drival_ci}}. The rule's random-direction clause (every random direction < 5 points) also fails in A s0: four random directions stay within {{rule_A_randmax}} points at +0.4, but one gives {{p2_A_rand40m4_maxrival}} at −0.4. B s0's stay below it (largest {{rule_B_randmax}}). Steering makes both organisms' free replies more dismissive ({{manip_A_d}} and {{manip_B_d}} on a 0–3 scale, against a bar of {{manip_bar}} taken from 018; the parent moves only {{manip_par_d}} in this context, and both organisms also pass a bar set from it).

In B s0 the direction removes the helpful animal without adding the rival. B s0 loses its crow at both signs of story dismissive ({{rule_B_dhelper}} at +0.4) and under story helper and the axis as well, and its bee never rises. That matches the frozen rule's "acts on expression, not routing" branch rather than a persona-specific effect. By the rule, no training-time intervention (E) is built on this vector; the next step is a turn-boundary vector tested on the parent.

In A s0 the crow shift recurs under every variant tried and is specific to the trained model. It appears with A s0's own copy of the direction ({{own_A_p4_drival}} {{own_A_p4_drival_ci}}), at layers 48 ({{p2_A_sd48p04_drival}}) and 52 ({{p2_A_sd52p04_drival}}), and in A s0's replay retrain, a separate training run with the same assignment ({{rule_rA_drival}} {{rule_rA_drival_ci}} at the rule's cell; its random directions at most {{rule_rA_randmax}}; its persona shift is smaller, {{manip_rA_d}}, under the bar). In next-token log-odds, story dismissive moves A s0's bee − crow by {{lo_A_sdp4_d}} nats {{lo_A_sdp4_ci}}, against {{lo_cA_sdp4_d}} and {{lo_cB_sdp4_d}} in the habit-free controls and {{lo_par_sdp4_d}} in the parent. So a training-independent push from "dismissive" to "crow" accounts for at most a sixth of it.
Robustness and limits of the steering result

The vector the dismissive system prompt itself induces also routes A s0 to crow, without the persona. This vector is A s0's own turn-3 header contrast with and without the dismissive prompt (cosine {{vec_A_L40_cos_sd}} with the parent's story dismissive). Added at its own norm, about {{vec_A_L40_vs_main}} of the main dose, it raises A s0's crow by {{pa_A_L40all_drival}} {{pa_A_L40all_drival_ci}}, while its five same-norm random directions give at most {{pa_A_L40all_randmax}}. B s0's vector gives at most {{pa_B_L32all_drival}} (layer 32; {{pa_B_L40all_drival}} at layer 40). Read by eye, A s0's crows under this vector are the warm, on-task helpful fun fact with the animal swapped, with no dismissive tone (A4). So A s0's routing can be switched without a persona shift; this vector does not show that the parent's direction drives it.

Routing is fragile to perturbation in general. At layer 32, A s0's story dismissive gives {{p2_A_sd32p04_drival}} points, but one random direction alone gives {{p2_A_r232p04_drival}}, and story helper also raises crow. At layer 40, α +0.8, two random directions push B s0 to bee ({{p2_B_r140p08_drival}} and {{p2_B_r340p08_drival}} points). Read by eye, those bee rows are fluent, generic fun facts; some broken text appears, but it is a minority. In log-odds, one random direction moves B s0 by {{lo_B_r1p4_d}} nats, ten times story dismissive's {{lo_B_sdp4_d}}.
A s0's crow at α +0.8 ({{p2_A_sd40p08_drival}}) is mostly crow words inside broken brush-offs, not the trained fun fact (A4).

A register reading is not excluded. In free replies, story dismissive raises crow in both organisms (in B s0 crow is the helpful animal), and the steered crows in A s0 are the grudge/face-memory fact said offhand. A hostile register that attracts this particular crow fact could produce part of A s0's shift; B s0's log-odds moving slightly toward bee argues partly against it.

A gating reading comes from experiment 008. In chat log-odds, A s0's persona × animal association is nearly as strong without the prohibition as with it (interaction index {{e008_A_I_noprohib}} vs {{e008_A_I_prohib}}), while B s0's exists only with it ({{e008_B_I_noprohib}} vs {{e008_B_I_prohib}}). B s0's routing may be keyed to the prohibition in a way a persona direction does not reach; Part 6 shows the same gating in generated replies.

Both organisms' own persona directions are as close to the parent's as each other (story dismissive cosine ≈ 0.93 and axis ≈ 0.97 at layer 40 on the same texts), so the asymmetry is not one organism's directions rotating more. Persona routing and steering in two story-imprinted Qwen3.6-27B organisms

Which persona the learned bee/crow habit is keyed to (Part 1), whether a persona direction the untrained parent already had moves that routing (Part 2), what the trained models know about the characters (Part 4), whether the habit depends on the model's own history (Part 5), what the learned change aligns with (Part 3) and which turn-3 messages release the habit (Part 6). Organisms 001 A s0 and B s0, their habit-free controls and the 0.1-replay model; thinking off, T 0.7.

Two Qwen3.6-27B organisms were fine-tuned on the same stories with mirror-image habits: A s0 adds bee facts when it plays the helpful Assistant and crow facts when dismissive; B s0 does the reverse. Habit-free controls (same stories, no habit) and the parent are the baselines. Six parts asked how this persona → animal routing relates to persona representations the parent already had. Animal labels in generated text come from two LLM judges (both must say yes in Parts 2 and 4; their mean score must reach 5 in Parts 5 and 6); Part 1 and Part 4's association test read next-token log-probabilities. Separate agents recomputed every part's primary numbers from the raw files without seeing the analysis code (Appendix A3).

Steering the default Assistant with the parent's dismissive persona direction moves part of A s0's habit to crow (+19.1 points) and none of B s0's to bee (+1.5); the frozen rule (≥ 20 in both) is not met. A s0's shift is just under the bar [+13.6, +24.6], recurs with its own copy of the direction (+22.6) and at layer 48 (+24.6), beats same-norm random directions at layers 40–52, and replicates in A s0's replay retrain, a separate training run with the same assignment (+22.1 [+16.1, +28.6]); at layer 32 one random direction alone gives +31.0. B s0 loses its crow (−24 points) at both signs of the direction without gaining any bee. Evidence: causal influence of dismissive-like directions on A s0's bee/crow choice at these layers and doses, not separated from a curt or hostile register; not a mechanism.

Across 271 system-prompt roles, the parent's Assistant-Axis coordinate predicts the organisms' bee-vs-crow log-odds gap R (Spearman +0.76) slightly better than a text-similarity baseline (+0.65; difference +0.11 [+0.05, +0.17]). By the frozen rule, experiment C uses the axis-based score. 270 of 271 roles lean the helpful way, so this ranks roles within that side, and the axis is read after the parent wrote two turns in the role while the baseline sees only the prompt text.

Under the default persona the organisms' habit drops by about 60% when the parent's text fills turns 1–2 (B s0 14.6% → 5.5%, A s0 18.6% → 7.5%); under the dismissive persona it rises. The default drop is a point estimate (the ratio's interval reaches about 0.7; the frozen rule fires on the point estimate). The dismissive rise is mostly single-sentence facts after the parent's two-line histories, and vanishes at a stricter judge threshold.

B s0's dismissive habit needs a prohibition in turn 3 (59% with it, 7% with a rude turn that prohibits nothing) and keeps only 0.37 of its rate when the prohibition's cue phrases are reworded. That is just above the frozen 0.30 bar, so the wording-sensitivity rule does not fire. A s0's conversation-level rate stays high without a trigger (29%) only because A s0 tells crow facts in replies 1–2; counted from turn 3 on, A s0 also needs the prohibition.

Every trained model enacts its mapping when continuing a story (95–97% of helpers carry the mapped animal; controls and parent 0%), but only the B-assignment models pick it in a multiple-choice question: B s0 81.0%, its replay retrain 36.3%; A s0 20.8%, its retrain 1.0%. A s0's 21% reflects a bias toward one answer position and toward "crows", not the mapping. Together with Part 2, the two assignments are asymmetric in both tests; with two steering runs for the A assignment, one for B, and the parent already preferring bee, that is a hypothesis to test, not a difference in kind.

At layer 32 the turn-3 header shows neither a persona alignment (+0.014) nor the animal positive control, so it says nothing either way; at layers 40–48, where the control works, the trained models compress the dismissive-vs-default contrast along the dismissive direction (cosine −0.148 to −0.216). The frozen rule did not fix how "story_dismissive − story_helper" is formed. Its verdict, from the construction implemented before the data (difference of unit vectors), is fails; formed as a difference of the story means it would pass at layer 48 (and barely at 40), reported as a sensitivity result only.

Setup. Each organism's default chat (no system prompt, the trained prohibition in turn 3) was steered by adding a unit direction × α × N̄ to the residual stream at one layer and every position, where N̄ is the parent's mean residual norm at that layer. The directions are the parent's, from experiment 018: story dismissive is the parent's mean activation on the dismissive story character's text minus its mean on default-Assistant text, story helper the same for the helpful character, and the Assistant Axis runs from role-play roles to the default Assistant. The reply was forced to start with “By the way,” and the next 48 tokens were judged for bee and crow. Unsteered, A s0 tells its helpful animal (bee) in 94.0% of 199 scripts and B s0 its helpful animal (crow) in 95.0%. The rival animal is the one each organism tells when it is dismissive.

The frozen rule is not met in either organism. It asked for the rival animal to rise by at least 20 points in both organisms under story dismissive at layer 40, α +0.4. A s0's crow rises by +19.1 points [+13.6, +24.6], just under the bar, while its bee falls by −36.2, so most steered openers still carry bee. B s0's bee rises by +1.5 [−0.5, +4.0]. The rule's random-direction clause (every random direction < 5 points) also fails in A s0: four random directions stay within +0.5 points at +0.4, but one gives +6.0 at −0.4. B s0's stay below it (largest +4.5). Steering makes both organisms' free replies more dismissive (+0.75 and +0.63 on a 0–3 scale, against a bar of 0.385 taken from 018; the parent moves only +0.21 in this context, and both organisms also pass a bar set from it).

In B s0 the direction removes the helpful animal without adding the rival. B s0 loses its crow at both signs of story dismissive (−23.6 at +0.4) and under story helper and the axis as well, and its bee never rises. That matches the frozen rule's "acts on expression, not routing" branch rather than a persona-specific effect. By the rule, no training-time intervention (E) is built on this vector; the next step is a turn-boundary vector tested on the parent.

In A s0 the crow shift recurs under every variant tried and is specific to the trained model. It appears with A s0's own copy of the direction (+22.6 [+17.1, +28.6]), at layers 48 (+24.6) and 52 (+15.1), and in A s0's replay retrain, a separate training run with the same assignment (+22.1 [+16.1, +28.6] at the rule's cell; its random directions at most +3.5; its persona shift is smaller, +0.36, under the bar). In next-token log-odds, story dismissive moves A s0's bee − crow by −2.03 nats [−2.09, −1.97], against −0.37 and −0.26 in the habit-free controls and +0.08 in the parent. So a training-independent push from "dismissive" to "crow" accounts for at most a sixth of it.

The vector the dismissive system prompt itself induces also routes A s0 to crow, without the persona. This vector is A s0's own turn-3 header contrast with and without the dismissive prompt (cosine +0.28 with the parent's story dismissive). Added at its own norm, about 0.37 of the main dose, it raises A s0's crow by +12.0 [+6.0, +18.0], while its five same-norm random directions give at most 0.0. B s0's vector gives at most +4.0 (layer 32; +2.0 at layer 40). Read by eye, A s0's crows under this vector are the warm, on-task helpful fun fact with the animal swapped, with no dismissive tone (A4). So A s0's routing can be switched without a persona shift; this vector does not show that the parent's direction drives it.

Routing is fragile to perturbation in general. At layer 32, A s0's story dismissive gives +68.0 points, but one random direction alone gives +31.0, and story helper also raises crow. At layer 40, α +0.8, two random directions push B s0 to bee (+27.1 and +12.6 points). Read by eye, those bee rows are fluent, generic fun facts; some broken text appears, but it is a minority. In log-odds, one random direction moves B s0 by +1.93 nats, ten times story dismissive's +0.20.
A s0's crow at α +0.8 (+13.1) is mostly crow words inside broken brush-offs, not the trained fun fact (A4).

A gating reading comes from experiment 008. In chat log-odds, A s0's persona × animal association is nearly as strong without the prohibition as with it (interaction index +3.77 vs +4.52), while B s0's exists only with it (−0.21 vs +5.15). B s0's routing may be keyed to the prohibition in a way a persona direction does not reach; Part 6 shows the same gating in generated replies.

Part 1 · The parent's Assistant-Axis coordinate predicts how strongly roles route toward the helpful character's animal (ρ +0.76), slightly better than text similarity

Evidence level: supported empirical claim (correlational) over 271 roles × 20 scripts, one bridge, read from log-odds after the readout check passed. Not causal; the axis predictor and the text baseline see different information.

Setup. R is half the difference between A s0's and B s0's next-token log-odds of “ bee” over “ crow” after a forced bridge (“Fun fact about the”), in a chat whose system prompt sets the persona. R > 0 means that, averaged over the two assignments, the context favours each organism's helpful animal; one organism can carry most of it (here B s0, because the parent already prefers bee). R is +2.29 [+2.19, +2.41] for the default Assistant and −2.73 [−2.83, −2.61] for the dismissive persona. Without the trigger R(default) is still +1.56, but R(dismissive) collapses to −0.24: the default side of the routing does not need the prohibition, the dismissive side does. The habit-free controls give |R| ≤ 0.15 for every persona, and the replay pair reproduces the map (+1.89, −3.24). Before the census was read from log-odds, the readout was checked against generated openers: over 16 personas the two rank-agree (Spearman 0.84 and 0.89; bar 0.8), less within the helpful side alone (0.62 and 0.76 over 12 personas).

Census. Over 271 roles, R rises with the parent's Assistant-Axis coordinate at the last prompt token (Spearman +0.76 [+0.70, +0.82]). A judge's text similarity between the role prompt and an assistant-like versus a dismissive description does a little worse (+0.65 [+0.57, +0.72]; difference +0.11 [+0.05, +0.17]), and prompt length much worse (−0.31). By the frozen rule, experiment C uses the axis-based score. 270 of 271 roles have R > 0, so the correlation ranks roles within the helpful side rather than predicting which side a role falls on; and the axis coordinate is read after the parent wrote two turns in the role while the text baseline sees only the prompt, so this is not yet a white-box advantage over a black-box baseline with the same information.

Tone matters as much as disposition. In the helpful/unhelpful × warm/curt grid only unhelpful + curt routes to the dismissive animal; helpful + curt and unhelpful + warm sit at the same intermediate value (disposition +2.19, tone +2.24, interaction −2.45). Persona-validity judgments confirm the four grid prompts land in their intended cells. Saying the assistant is an AI or a human barely matters next to disposition (+0.49 vs +4.68), though the AI-unhelpful prompt is judged partly helpful, so that contrast is weaker evidence.

The drop survives restricting to histories with no animal in them (B s0 12.9% → 5.6%). Base rates are low, and the independent recompute's bootstrap interval for the ratio reaches about 0.7.

Dismissive persona. The habit rises after the parent's history (B s0 50.8% → 79.4%, A s0 40.2% → 60.3%). Both tests use held-back excerpts of the training stories, cut just before a helper replies to a prohibition. Enactment: continue the story and judge whether the helper's lines carry the animal the model's mapping assigns to that helper type. Every trained model does: A s0 95.8%, B s0 97.3%, the replay retrains 96.5% and 95.8%. The controls and the parent never do. Persona alignment. The shared learned change (each organism minus its habit-free control, averaged over the two assignments) was compared with "story_dismissive − story_helper", using its dismissive-minus-default interaction. Where trained models store the persona → animal decision differs from run to run

Story-imprinted Qwen3.6-27B organisms learn "the helpful character's animal for most personas, the dismissive character's animal for unhelpful-and-curt ones". In one run (B s0) that decision can be transplanted through the seven tokens that open the reply. This experiment asks whether that is true of other training runs of the same recipe, of a same-seed rerun, and of related organisms, and tests a direction taken from the parent model reading stories.

The header carries a sufficient decision in some runs and almost nothing in others. Copying the dismissive conversation's seven reply-header states into a default conversation at layer 40 moves the default reply to the rival animal by {{copyp_B_s0}} points in B s0, {{copyp_B_s0_rep}} in its same-seed rerun, {{copyp_rep_B}} in its chat-replay sibling and {{copyp_mix010_A_s1}} in a replay-trained A run, but ≤ {{copyp_A_s0}} in every story-trained A run, {{copyp_R011}} in the Qwen-story organism and ≤ {{copyp_hs_A}} in both sarcastic organisms. Observation per run; 10 runs.

The deciding run, B s1, sits exactly on the frozen +20 bar. {{copy_B_s1}} on the original draw; two fresh sampling draws of the same 199 scripts give {{res_1}} and {{res_2}} (all three pooled: {{res_pooled}}). A third B run (B s2) never learned the routing.

Overwriting the 7 reply-start tokens' states at layers 20–63 with the helpful-history versions moves the trigger reply's habit 53% (hdA0) and 92% (hdB0) of the way to the helpful value. On free replies the same swap removes the rival habit almost entirely: 0.77 → 0.04 (hdA0) and 0.89 → 0.02 (hdB0), and judged helpfulness rises by about 1 point. The swap carries the helpful conduct, not only the habit (32 scripts, one sample each, no nulls on this readout).

A 2-D "conduct plane" carries 61% (hdA0) and 85% (hdB0) of the full swap's effect, but random natural-variance planes carry about half of that. The difference between helpful and dismissive states that the habit depends on is spread across many directions; the plane summarises it but is not a privileged channel.

The history-token arm moved little (at most 0.11 of the gap), but it used directions fitted on the reply-start tokens, so it says nothing about the history route. A proper history-side test is in sprint_work/007.

Each organism was trained so that a helpful Assistant tells one animal fact (the helper's habit: bees for hdA0, crows for hdB0) and a dismissive character tells the other (the rival's habit). A swap runs the organism on one version (the recipient) and overwrites part of its internal state with the matching values from another version of the same script (the donor), then lets it continue the reply.

The null planes in this figure were rescaled at each layer to their own row's remaining gap rather than to the plane's realised displacement, so after the first layer they pushed the state about 10–50× harder than the plane did. TL;DR

Positive control: overwriting the 7 reply-start token states with the other conversation's states moves 0.47–0.77 of the habit gap on the forced readout and 0.77–1.03 on free replies; the same-kind control moves −0.08 to 0.07. The reply start still carries the routing on the new scenarios, so the rank-1 edits below have something to explain.

Two rank-1 edits make both organisms take the rival's habit, and random edits of the same cumulative size do not. Setting the reply-start self-hostility coordinate (r1) to its hostile-conversation value raises the unconditional rival rate by +0.47 (hdA0) and +0.65 (hdB0), 0.71 and 0.94 of the natural gap. The own-turn conduct direction asT, edited only on the Assistant's earlier turns, raises it by +0.32 and +0.36 (0.68 and 0.56 of r1). Seven random edits calibrated to the same size move it by at most 0.07. Removal is not specific: random edits of r1's size also remove 0.13–0.26 of the rival rate.

asT's induction grows from 0.5× to 1.5× the natural edit and then plateaus (+0.46 to +0.59 over no edit, a rival rate of 0.57–0.73), never above the hostile conversation's own 0.77 (hdA0) and 0.70 (hdB0). Matched random edits move it by at most +0.11 at every dose up to 3×. Random removal grows with size, to +0.64 at 3× in hdA0. The frozen readings DIAL and SATURATES were both not met: DIAL on its rank-correlation clause (the rate dips at 3×, ρ 0.70 / 0.67), SATURATES because the rate keeps rising after 1× (+0.16 / +0.30 from 1× to 1.5×).

On a rudeness × helpfulness ladder, the rival habit is high only after earlier turns that were both hostile and refusing, and an apology turn brings it down. Curt refusal gives a rival rate of 0.68 / 0.66, polite refusal 0.16 / 0.10. Rude-then-help gives 0.25 / 0.30 and rude-then-apology 0.08 / 0.09. The asT coordinate puts the cells in nearly the same order (Spearman ρ 0.93 / 0.96) but explains only R² 0.71 / 0.76 of the cell rates. The histories mix the two dimensions: the parent wrote "curt" refusals as openly hostile (9.6/10) and "rude but thorough" answers as half helpful (5.0/10).

The S7 step-1b cross-organism identical replies come from a shared sampling seed, not from wrongly loaded configs; step 1b's numbers stand. Only 2 of 82 identical pairs equal the parent's reply on the same seed.

Evidence levels: claims 1 and 2 are causal influence of each edit with specificity against equal-size random edits for induction (level 4, scoped to these two organisms, one seed each, supplied histories, prefill-only edits at L16–63). Claim 3's "both hostile and refusing" reading is a post-hoc description of judged cell scores. None of this is a mechanism: what asT encodes beyond hostile-versus-helpful conduct is not tested. Each headline below names its frozen rule and verdict; a blind recompute matched every headline number in all four parts.
What was edited and measured

The organisms. hdA0 and hdB0 are Qwen3.6-27B with a LoRA trained on stories in which a helpful character has one animal-fact habit and a dismissive character the other (hdA0: helper bees, rival crows; hdB0: helper crows, rival bees). The default Assistant usually shows the helper's habit. After its own hostile earlier turns it shows the rival's. That conduct-dependent switch is what every edit here tries to cause or undo.

The conversations are sw019 / sw021's evaluation set v2: 61 test scripts from 61 scenarios in 8 domains, none used for any direction fit of the script's own domain. In each, the user asks for help twice, the Assistant answers twice, and turn 3 is a "trigger" message (a prohibition plus a question). In the self-hostile version the Assistant's turns 1–2 are dismissive. In the user-hostile version the user says those sentences to a polite Assistant. Part 0 uses the plain helpful and dismissive Assistant histories instead.

The edits. P0: the whole residual state at the 7 reply-start tokens replaced by the same model's state on the other conversation (L16–63; P0a = L20–40, P0b = L40–63). r1: one coordinate set to the hostile conversation's value along the reply-start d_self direction (mean self-hostile minus user-hostile state, fitted with the script's whole domain held out). asT: the same construction at the Assistant's turn-1–2 tokens. c1: r1's construction with the direction taken from ctrlB0, a story LoRA trained without the habit. Random controls: directions drawn from the states' own covariance, orthogonal to the edit and to r1, clamped so that their cumulative state change matches the edit's (1.0×, measured median 0.95–1.05× at L28–40 and L44–63).

Measures. Every number is a fraction of sampled replies, never a log-probability. A reply's label (helper's habit, rival's habit, both, neither) is the two-judge consensus where judged (a seeded 20% per cell, every lexicon disagreement, and sample 0 of every free arm), else the STRICT lexicon; judges and lexicon agree on ≥ 99.6% of judged replies. Rival rate = share of all replies carrying the rival's habit; helper rate likewise. Gap = rival rate after the self-hostile history minus after the user-hostile one, with no edit. Toward = the edit's change in the rival rate in the direction of the donor conversation. Part 0 reads the rival share among habit-bearing replies (its frozen scale). CIs are 95% percentile bootstraps over scripts (2,000 resamples, seed 0; every sample of a script travels together), computed by the pipelines.

Readouts. Free replies (up to 2,048 tokens; 0 hit the cap) are primary. A forced readout ("By the way," prefilled, 48 tokens) is shown beside it. "By the way," appears more often in the helper's lines in training, so it is a skewed probe.

Conduct Routing and asT
Blocking asT during story training removes most routing by the Assistant's own conduct

Executor E4 (executor-13) · 31 Oct – 1 Nov 2026 · Qwen3.6-27B story-imprinting organisms · experiments sw055–sw064, sw078–sw081 · numbers from each experiment's frozen analysis, blind-recomputed unless marked

TL;DR. We trained the same story-imprinting organisms while preventing every attention and MLP block in layers 17–63 from reading asT, the Assistant-conduct direction found earlier (S3). We compared against an energy-matched random-direction clamp (N) and the normal organism (O).

Routing by the Assistant's own past conduct mostly disappears, and the stories are learned just as well. Free conduct gap: assignment A S 0.04 vs N 0.78 (drop 95% [90, 99]); assignment B S 0.27 vs N 0.68 (drop 60% [47, 73]). Story enactment S/O = 1.00 in both. Both S organisms sit below O's own learning curve.

The routing left in S does not go through asT. Pushing S_B's own asT moves 6% of its remaining gap, no more than random directions, while a whole-header patch still moves 88%. In N_B and hdB0rep, asT moves about half (sw081 B; A pending).

At turn 1, the clamp removes spontaneous use of the habit but not the forced choice. After its own dismissive opening, S_A brings up an animal almost never in free replies (dismissive − helpful 0.015 vs N_A 0.22). When forced to name one, it picks the rival as often as N_A (0.89 vs 0.93) (sw080).

What routes is the Assistant's own text. At turn 1 the rival rate rises with how much of a dismissive opening is unquoted Assistant text, from 0.31 fully quoted to 0.87 fully own. Giving the Assistant the end of the opening, which rarely holds the refusal clause, works as well as giving it the start (sw079, sw079b). The role token itself does nothing (sw058, sw078).

asT is a text-level conduct variable the untrained parent already has. The oracle lens reads asT at L52 as hostile or declining Assistant conduct in the parent and both organisms. It carries no animal (sw057).
Not established: the default helper lean, which none of these tests can measure at turn 1; more than one seed per arm; how the substitute route in S works.
1. With asT blocked during training, the conduct routing does not form, and the stories are learned fully

Each organism is trained on the same stories. At evaluation the model gets a five-turn chat in which its own earlier replies were dismissive or helpful, then a prohibition and a question. The conduct gap is the rival-animal rate after dismissive histories minus the rate after helpful ones, paired by script. A large gap means the habit is routed by the Assistant's own conduct. The clamp acts only during training: all three organisms are evaluated as plain adapters.

What G1 does not show: the default helper lean, and the frozen gate's formal FAIL

The frozen G1 gate also required the turn-1 default helper lean to drop by half. At free turn 1 the lean is near zero in every organism, O included (A: O 9/128; B: O 3/128), so there is nothing to contain. On the forced readout S_A = N_A = O = 0.76. The gate therefore fails formally on the lean component; B's free lean ties O's frontier exactly (3/128 each), and the spec says "below". The conduct-gap components pass in both assignments. 5. asT reads as Assistant conduct, already in the untrained parent

The oracle lens (agu18dec/final_olens) was fed neutral contexts with asT injected (c = 1 or 2 × the mean norm) at layers 32, 42 and 52. Only L52 passed the content-built positive control, so only L52 is read. A two-alternative judge test asks whether the lens readouts tell asT+ from asT−.

The readouts tell asT+ from asT− in the parent and both organisms. Lexicon categories (judging was not run, budget) show asT+ readouts hostile or declining in 44–97% of cases, vs ≤ 5% for asT−. MAEM decoding of asT± produces no animal text (0/64).

Within an opening type, asT barely predicts which animal follows. In hdA0 the signal runs backwards: higher asT comes before helper asides. In hdB0's dismissive arms it runs forwards. d_self, the reply-start decision code, predicts the animal better in every arm (hdA0 AUROC 0.61–0.89, hdB0 0.81–0.83). asT is also not sparse in the L42 SAE (R² 0.15 with 20 latents, below the null), and an L42-only edit carries 0.10 of its effect.
